title: Structure: Architecting the Argument
subtitle: From raw thinking to a spine that carries a room
outcome: Take a messy pile of thinking and turn it into a single load-bearing claim with a named structure - SCQA, a StoryCircle, or a deductive pyramid - that you can defend in the first sixty seconds and in the follow-up questions.
abstract: Most executives are not bad speakers. They are untidy thinkers with good instincts, and they let their decks do the thinking for them. This module treats argument structure as a design problem with named, repeatable solutions rather than a matter of taste. It introduces Barbara Minto's Pyramid Principle and SCQA, shows exactly how a deductive spine differs from a narrative arc, and teaches the diagnostic that finds a buried conclusion before the room does: the Reverse Outline. It adds Toulmin's claim-evidence-warrant, the So-What Ladder for driving a claim until it bears weight, and Dan Harmon's StoryCircle as the decision-shaped alternative to argument. Every technique here is executable in under 40 minutes on a real, upcoming talk, and every framework is designed to be reused rather than admired.
objectives: Distinguish Barbara Minto's deductive Pyramid Principle from an inductive narrative arc, and select the correct architecture for a given room and a given kind of decision.
Construct a four-part SCQA opening that makes the recommendation feel inevitable rather than asserted, and know when SCQA is the wrong tool.
Climb the So-What Ladder until a claim becomes load-bearing, and cut the material that never reaches the top.
Name the warrant in a claim-evidence-warrant argument, so the audience is not asked to do the connecting work for you.
Write a one-page spine before opening a slide tool, and enforce the one-idea-per-talk constraint with tests that fail loudly.
Diagnose a buried conclusion with the Reverse Outline and repair it by leading with the answer and supporting it afterwards.

keyTerms.definition: Barbara Minto's rule that a business argument should be deductive and top-down: the answer at the apex, mutually exclusive and collectively exhaustive arguments beneath it.
Minto's term for the single sentence that states the conclusion at the top of the pyramid - a position, not a topic.
Mutually exclusive and collectively exhaustive: Minto's grouping rule, requiring that arguments within a group do not overlap and that the groups together cover the question completely.
Situation, Complication, Question, Answer: Minto's four-part structure for the opening of a business argument, in which the answer follows the derivation of the question.
The repeated test of asking 'so what?' of each statement, climbing until the claim reaches the level where it would change a decision.
A claim whose removal would change the recommendation; the top of the spine, as opposed to a fact that merely sits in the talk.
Stephen Toulmin's three-part structure for an argument, in which the warrant is the bridge that makes the evidence relevant to the claim.
The usually unspoken reasoning that connects cited evidence to the claim being made - and the step most business arguments omit.
A single-page plan holding the governing thought, the ask, the supporting arguments, the evidence, and the counter-argument, written before any slide exists.
A diagnostic in which every paragraph or section is summarised in one line, and the summaries are then read on their own to reveal the argument the document actually makes.
The failure mode in which the recommendation appears late, hedged, or implied, so the room must reconstruct it from the evidence.
Leading with the answer and supporting it afterwards - bottom line up front in military usage, the inverted pyramid in journalism, the governing thought in Minto's usage.
Dan Harmon's eight-beat description of story structure, adapted here as a decision arc: a character with a want meets resistance and escalates toward a new equilibrium.
The narrative shape of a decision being made under resistance, used when the task is to move people toward change rather than to adjudicate a recommendation.

concepts.title: The Pyramid Principle Is Not a Story, and Your Talk Cannot Be Both
concepts.summary: Barbara Minto trained at McKinsey in the 1970s and published The Pyramid Principle in 1987. Its rule is that business argument is deductive and top-down: the answer at the apex, mutually exclusive and collectively exhaustive arguments beneath. A narrative arc is the opposite architecture - inductive, chronological, and dependent on withholding the destination. Both are legitimate. Confusing them is the most common structural error in executive talks.
concepts.detail:
Minto reverse-engineered the Pyramid Principle from what senior audiences do to weak presentations: they interrupt and ask 'so what are you asking me to do?' The answer is that a business argument should be deductive. The governing thought sits at the apex - a position, never a topic - and beneath it sit the MECE arguments that support it, grouped so each group is complete in itself and the groups together cover the question. Crucially, the top of the pyramid is a conclusion. A reader should never be able to finish your document and mistake 'the state of the enterprise cloud market' for your position on it.

A narrative arc is the opposite architecture, and the opposition is structural rather than stylistic. Narrative is inductive: chronological moments accumulate, meaning emerges from sequence and tension, and the conclusion is a retrospective rather than a premise. Campbell's monomyth and Pixar's story spine - 'once upon a time... every day... until one day...' - are narrative technologies that buy attention by withholding the destination. Minto's pyramid withholds nothing; it front-loads the destination and then earns it.

Both are legitimate, and choosing between them is a design decision rather than a matter of taste:

| | Pyramid (deductive) | Narrative (inductive) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Answer appears | First, within 30-60 seconds | Last, at the closing line |
| Listener's job | Evaluate a stated claim | Track a changing situation |
| Best for | Decisions, recommendations, audits, comparisons | Change adoption, origin stories, culture, loss, new-category framing |
| Failure mode | Sounds like a memo read aloud | Sounds evasive in a room that wants a decision |

The common failure is a hybrid that serves neither: a dramatic war story that opens the talk, an argument that never arrives, and a conclusion that turns up on slide 14 by accident. If you need both, use them in sequence rather than interleaved. Spend two minutes on the situation and the conflict, state the answer, then support it deductively. Nancy Duarte's Resonate (2010) describes the same movement as oscillating between 'what is' - the status quo - and 'what could be' - the possibility, with the talk's job to hold both in tension. That is narrative energy wrapped around a deductive structure, and it is cleaner than telling a story and hoping it lands somewhere.
principles: Decide deliberately between a deductive spine and an inductive arc before you write a single slide; the two have opposite opening moves and cannot be interleaved.
State the conclusion as a position, not a topic - if your top-line sentence could be a chapter heading, it is not a governing thought.
Group your arguments MECE: within a group they must not overlap, and across groups they must cover the question completely.
If you need both modes, run them in sequence - narrative setup first, then the deductive argument - rather than weaving them together.
Treat 'sounds like a memo read aloud' as a design defect, not a delivery defect; the fix is ordering and evidence, not vocal variety.

pitfalls.failure: Starting a decision meeting with a three-minute origin story, so the room spends its peak attention on your history rather than the decision in front of it.
pitfalls.fix: Move the origin story to the Situation line of an SCQA, compressed to two sentences, and state the recommendation before minute one.

pitfalls.failure: Presenting a topic rather than a claim at the top - 'On pricing strategy' - which forces the audience to infer your position.
pitfalls.fix: Rewrite the title as a sentence with a verb and a direction: 'We should raise prices on self-serve tiers to 8 percent'.

pitfalls.failure: Running a narrative arc in a room that wants a decision, so the talk ends with an inspiring story and no ask.
pitfalls.fix: Ask in the first minute what decision is being made. If there is one, the structure is deductive and the story becomes illustration.

pitfalls.failure: Over-grouping: seven arguments in a three-bucket hierarchy, so the buckets do not cover the question and the arguments do not exclude each other.
pitfalls.fix: Test coverage by asking what a sceptical colleague would say is missing. If they can name it, the group is not exhaustive.

concepts.title: SCQA: The Frame Business Rooms Actually Ask For
concepts.summary: SCQA - Situation, Complication, Question, Answer - is Minto's answer to how to open. Situation establishes shared context, Complication establishes what changed, Question derives what must be asked, and Answer is where you land before supporting it. It is a compression device rather than a storytelling device, which is exactly why it wins in decision rooms and fails in rooms that do not yet share your context.
concepts.detail:
The order in SCQA is load-bearing. If the Answer comes before the Complication, the audience cannot evaluate it, because they do not yet understand why it is needed. Situation states what the audience already accepts - the market, the plan, the constraint, the timeline. Complication states what is now true that makes the situation a problem. Question is what the situation and complication force someone to ask. Answer is your response, and it is where you land before you support it.

SCQA is a compression device, not a storytelling device. It assumes the audience is already inside the argument's world and wants to be told what to do about a specific problem. That assumption is precisely what makes it right for some rooms and wrong for others.

Use SCQA when the audience shares your context and wants a decision; when the situation is contested or has changed and needs a fresh frame; or when the reader will read once and act - board pre-reads, memos, budget requests, approval asks. Its signature strength is that it makes the ask feel inevitable rather than chosen, because the question was derived from the complication instead of asserted.

Do not use SCQA when the audience does not yet share the context: a conference room of strangers, a new market, a first all-hands, an external keynote. Situation becomes a lecture and you burn your peak attention on things the room either knows or ignores. Do not use it when the belief itself is the problem - a Situation that says 'here is how the world works' will be rejected along with everything else if the world view is what the room disputes. Do not use it when the emotion is the message: a layoff, a death in the organisation, a plant closing. Those rooms need a human moment before a structural one.

The most common misuse is a Situation that is really an agenda. 'As you know, we have been growing steadily over the last three quarters' is context, not Situation. A Situation is the minimum the audience needs in order to understand why the Complication matters: one or two sentences. If it needs a slide, it is too long.

One final test on the Complication: if the audience would not agree that the Complication is a problem, you are about to spend twenty minutes arguing a premise they have not accepted, and you will lose the room before you reach the Answer. Find out what they think before you build the SCQA. The Audience Contract from Module 1 is the input to this framework.
principles: Situation must be the minimum context the room needs to understand the Complication - two sentences, never a slide.
Derive the Question from the Complication; a Question asserted rather than derived is the most common sign of a manufactured urgency.
Land the Answer before minute one in any decision room, then spend the remainder earning it.
Write the whole SCQA in four lines on one page before you open a slide tool.
Test the Complication by asking whether a sceptical member of the target room would agree it is a problem.

pitfalls.failure: A Situation written as a history lesson - three paragraphs of context the room already holds.
pitfalls.fix: Compress to the shortest claim that makes the Complication intelligible. If you cannot compress it, the Complication is not specific enough to be interesting.

pitfalls.failure: Stating the Answer first with no Complication, so it reads as an order rather than a conclusion the situation demands.
pitfalls.fix: Insert one sentence of Complication between Situation and Answer. That single sentence converts a demand into a finding.

pitfalls.failure: Using SCQA in a room that does not share the context - a first all-hands or a customer conference - and spending four minutes establishing the world.
pitfalls.fix: Compress Situation to a single clause and spend the time on the Complication and the stake. Or use a StoryCircle instead, which builds context through change rather than description.

pitfalls.failure: Leaving the Question implied so that the room cannot tell whether it is a question or a topic.
pitfalls.fix: State it as a question in the room's own words. The question is the hinge of the whole talk, so it should be the most careful sentence you write.

concepts.title: The So-What Ladder: Climbing Until the Claim Bears Weight
concepts.summary: The 'so what?' test is the cheapest and most brutal editing tool in executive speaking. Ask it of each statement, one rung at a time, until you reach a claim whose falsity would change somebody's behaviour. Most raw material dies on the second rung, which is how you discover what you actually think rather than what you happened to type.
concepts.detail:
Take any statement in your argument and ask the question out loud, one rung at a time. Each answer is a rung. The ladder ends when the claim is load-bearing: a claim whose removal changes the recommendation. 'We raised prices 8 percent in March' is a fact. 'Revenue per account rose 11 percent' is an interpretation. 'We should extend the increase to two more tiers' is an implication. 'So we should not build the discount tool we scoped last month' is the decision. That last statement is load-bearing: if it were false, the plan would change. Everything below it is support.

The ladder has three properties that make it work on a live stage. First, it is fast: each rung is one sentence, and most executives can climb a claim to load-bearing in four or five rungs. Second, it is falsifiable at every rung, which forces you to specify what you mean - 'adoption improved' becomes 'weekly active accounts rose from 40 percent to 61 percent of new logos'. Third, and most usefully, it makes your reasoning visible. When you deliver the ladder out loud, the room hears not just your conclusion but the path that produced it, which is where trust in a recommendation lives.

There are two failure modes. The first is over-climbing: continuing to ask 'so what?' until the statement becomes a trivial truth such as 'the business needs revenue' or 'customers want value'. Stop when the claim is load-bearing, not when it is universal. The test for stopping is whether the statement changes a decision someone in the room is about to make. The second failure is climbing the wrong claim. A supporting detail - a metric, a market statistic - can generate an infinite ladder that never reaches your recommendation. Climb the governing claim, and treat supporting evidence as endpoints rather than as rungs.

Richard Rumelt's Good Strategy Bad Strategy (2011) offers a useful companion: a strategy kernel is a diagnosis, a guiding policy, and coherent action. The diagnosis is the load-bearing sentence. If you cannot climb to a diagnosis that changes what you would do next week, you have a topic, not a strategy.

Practically, the ladder is also a live-room tool. When a CFO asks 'so what?' of your evidence, the question is not scepticism, it is a request for the rung you forgot to say. Answer with the next rung - not with more evidence.
principles: Ask 'so what?' until the claim changes a decision someone in the room is about to make; that is where you stop.
Make every rung falsifiable - vagueness hides a missing rung.
Climb the governing claim, not a supporting statistic; statistics are endpoints, not rungs.
Deliver the ladder out loud so the room hears the path, not just the conclusion.
When a listener asks 'so what?', answer with the next rung rather than with more evidence.

pitfalls.failure: Over-climbing to triviality - 'so what?' until you arrive at 'we need to make money' - which sounds impressive and carries no information.
pitfalls.fix: Set the stop rule in advance: the rung must name a decision, an owner, or a date. If it does not, you have climbed too far.

pitfalls.failure: Climbing a supporting detail instead of the claim, so the ladder produces a clever aside that never connects to the recommendation.
pitfalls.fix: Circle back to the governing claim before continuing. Every rung must be a step toward it.

pitfalls.failure: Never running the ladder at all, so the talk opens with a metric and the audience has to guess why you care about it.
pitfalls.fix: Run the ladder on your opening evidence before you write the opening. Two rungs is usually enough to find the point.

pitfalls.failure: Treating 'so what?' as an objection and defending the evidence instead of climbing.
pitfalls.fix: The question is a request for a rung, not a challenge. Say the next rung out loud and the tension dissolves.

concepts.title: Claim, Evidence, Warrant: Naming the Step You Usually Skip
concepts.summary: Stephen Toulmin's The Uses of Argument (1959) gives the oldest and sharpest analytical tool most executives have never read. Its claim, grounds, and warrant describe an argument properly - and the warrant, the bridge that makes evidence relevant to a claim, is the step nearly every business talk omits.
concepts.detail:
A full Toulmin argument has six parts: claim (what you assert), grounds or evidence (the facts you cite), warrant (the bridge that makes those facts relevant to the claim), backing (the support for the warrant), qualifier (the hedge that calibrates the strength), and rebuttal (the condition that would defeat the argument).

The part business talks skip is the warrant. 'We should raise prices 8 percent' plus 'our two nearest competitors raised prices 10 percent last quarter' is not an argument, because nothing connects the second to the first. The missing warrant looks like this: we sell into the same segment, our gross margin structure sits within two points of theirs, and their pricing change therefore signals willingness to pay rather than a clearance. Stated, the argument becomes arguable and checkable. Unstated, the audience must supply it themselves - and a room of executives will either supply it generously or notice that it is missing. You do not get to choose which.

This explains the commonest paradox in executive speaking: smart, well-evidenced talks that fail. The evidence is real, the recommendation is sound, but the audience was asked to do the connecting work, and executive attention is too expensive to spend on connecting. Every sentence that jumps from evidence to claim without a warrant is a sentence that asks the room to trust you slightly more than it needs to.

Warrant also explains why two talks with identical data land differently. Talk A: 'Churn is 14 percent, so we need to fix onboarding, so let us fund the two-person pod.' Talk B: 'Churn is 14 percent, and 60 percent of churn sits in accounts with fewer than five users. The five-user threshold is where self-serve setup breaks down, which is exactly what the onboarding pod addresses. So we should fund the pod.' Same data, same recommendation; B wins because it names the mechanism, and the mechanism is the warrant made visible.

Qualifiers and rebuttals are where credibility lives. 'Prices, excluding enterprise contracts, should rise 8 percent' is qualified - and stating the exclusion yourself makes it credible rather than evasive. 'Unless enterprise is more than 30 percent of revenue, in which case we hold' is a rebuttal, and volunteering it costs you nothing that the room's own objection would not have cost you anyway.
principles: After every piece of evidence, say the sentence that connects it to the claim - the warrant - out loud.
Name the mechanism, not just the number: why does this fact bear on this decision?
Volunteer the qualifier and the rebuttal before the room does; stated limits read as rigour.
Use backing when the warrant is contestable: state the assumption and its source.
Distrust any talk of yours that moves from a number to a recommendation without an intervening sentence.

pitfalls.failure: Treating a correlation as a warrant - 'customers who used the new onboarding churned less, so the onboarding pod will reduce churn'.
pitfalls.fix: Name the mechanism and its assumption: what specifically about the pod causes the reduction, and what would have to be true for that to hold?

pitfalls.failure: Omitting the warrant and reading the room's silence as agreement rather than as a gap in the argument.
pitfalls.fix: When you hear a question that sounds like 'how do you get from that to that', you have found the missing warrant. Say it explicitly.

pitfalls.failure: Dropping the qualifier to sound stronger, which costs credibility the moment a knowledgeable listener spots it.
pitfalls.fix: Keep the qualifier. 'For self-serve tiers, excluding enterprise, we should raise to 8 percent' is stronger because it is precise.

pitfalls.failure: Over-building the warrant until the talk becomes a lecture on method, with the recommendation pushed off the end.
pitfalls.fix: One sentence per warrant, then return to the argument. If the warrant needs a slide, it may be a genuine constraint worth surfacing - name it as such.

concepts.title: The One-Page Spine: Design the Argument Before You Open the Slide Tool
concepts.summary: The slide deck is the most seductive way to avoid thinking, because it produces the shape of a talk before it produces a thought. Open PowerPoint and you get a title slide, an agenda slide, and a rising sense of progress - none of which is an argument. The remedy is a one-page spine written before the deck exists, plus a one-idea constraint the spine forces.
concepts.detail:
The one-page spine has six fields, and it must fit on one page:

1. **Governing thought** - one sentence, the answer, stated as a position.
2. **The ask** - who does what, by when.
3. **The three arguments** - each a claim, in parallel form, MECE.
4. **The evidence** - one item per argument, each checkable.
5. **The counter-argument** - the strongest objection you will address yourself.
6. **Opening line and closing line**, written out.

If it does not fit on a page, it is not loaded. This is the same discipline as the one-page plan in Module 1, applied to structure rather than delivery.

The **one-idea constraint** is the spine's real work. A talk has one idea, not three, and there are five tests that make a violation fail loudly:

- **Hallway test**: write the one sentence you want repeated afterwards. If you cannot write it, you do not yet have an idea.
- **Which-one test**: if a listener could reasonably ask 'so which of these should we do?' and you cannot answer without hesitating, the ideas are not one idea.
- **Argument-count test**: more than three arguments is two talks. Four arguments is a book.
- **Parallel test**: if your arguments are not in the same grammatical form, they are not peers, and the room cannot hold them as a set.
- **Reverse-Outline test** (next concept): if your paragraph summaries do not add up to one sentence, you have more than one talk in your mouth.

One warning about sequence. Slides produce a shape before they produce a thought, and the shape then constrains the thought - you find yourself making a deck about three things because a three-column template was open. Daniel Bullock, Jacqueline Horn and Stephen Weil documented this effect in their 2010 Academy of Management Annals case study of consulting presentations, describing the dense, templated 'McKinsey way' slide as a genre that often carries the appearance of analysis without the argument. The deck shapes the thinking; the argument should shape the deck.

One practical rule: write **action titles**. Each slide title should be the point of the slide as a sentence - 'Enterprise onboarding is where we lose 60 percent of churn' rather than 'Onboarding'. Minto introduced the term for good reason: a title that states a claim forces the slide to have one, and a room reading titles aloud will reconstruct your argument even if they miss a word of the talk.
principles: Write the one-page spine before opening any slide tool, and let the deck serve it rather than generate it.
Cap the talk at one idea and three arguments; more is two talks, and two talks is one too many.
Give every slide an action title that states its point as a sentence, not a label.
Keep the arguments in parallel grammatical form so the room can hold them as a single set.
Rewrite the title of the deck itself as a claim - that is the cheapest test of whether you have a spine.

pitfalls.failure: Starting in the slide tool, so the deck's template - three columns, five sections - decides how many ideas the talk has.
pitfalls.fix: One page of text first. If you cannot write the six fields, you are not ready to design slides, because you do not yet know what the slides are for.

pitfalls.failure: Three arguments that are really one argument in three costumes - a cause, its symptom, and its consequence.
pitfalls.fix: Apply the So-What Ladder across the three. If argument two is the answer to 'so what?' about argument one, they are one argument.

pitfalls.failure: Naming slides as topics so the room must reconstruct your point while also listening to you.
pitfalls.fix: Convert every title to an action title. Then read only the titles aloud: if the argument does not survive that, it will not survive the talk.

pitfalls.failure: Treating the one-page limit as a formatting preference and letting the spine expand to three pages as the talk grows.
pitfalls.fix: The limit is the design constraint. When it overflows, you have found a second talk - cut it, or defer it to the written follow-up.

concepts.title: The Reverse Outline and the Buried Conclusion
concepts.summary: The Reverse Outline is the cheapest diagnostic in this module and the fastest way to find out whether your talk has a spine. Summarise every paragraph in one line, then read the summaries on their own. Whatever conclusion the room would draw from the summaries is the conclusion your talk actually makes - and if it is not the one you intended, you have found a buried conclusion.
concepts.detail:
Take the finished draft, the memo, or a transcript of your last talk. Write one line per paragraph: what that paragraph is for. Then read only the lines, in order, as though they were the talk - the compression your audience runs anyway, whether you help it or not. If the summaries add up to your recommendation, the talk works. If they add up to a description of the market, a history of the problem, or a series of observations, then the room is planning to draw its own conclusion, and it will draw it differently than you would.

A worked example. Three paragraphs: 'Sales growth has slowed for three consecutive quarters, from 14 percent to 4 percent. The slowdown is concentrated in enterprise deals, where our cycle time has doubled since the security review was added. We believe the security review is the primary cause.' The summaries read: 'Sales have slowed' / 'The slowdown is in enterprise' / 'The security review is the likely cause'. Read alone, they tell a diagnostic story - something is wrong - not an argument for a decision. If the talk was meant to ask for a staffing change to the security team, the conclusion is buried three paragraphs deep. Repair: lead with 'We need two security engineers to stop losing enterprise deals', then use the three paragraphs as the reasons it follows.

This is the anti-pattern that damages senior presenters most, and it has a name in the trade: the **buried conclusion**. Its variants are familiar: the recommendation arrives at minute 18 of 20; it is softened to 'we might want to explore whether'; it is stated as a question ('so should we consider staffing?') so that the room must supply the commitment; or it is presented as one of several options so that nobody owns it. In each case the presenter has handed the decision back to the audience without noticing.

**Induction versus deduction.** Academic and scientific writing is usually inductive: data first, conclusion last, with the reader deriving the finding. It is beautiful to read in a journal and lethal in a board meeting. Executives want deduction: the answer, then the reasons. The exception is exploratory work where you genuinely do not know the answer and the room's value is in the discovery - then say so explicitly, and front-load the finding anyway, because a finding and a conclusion are not the same object.

**Reverse the pyramid.** Lead with the answer and support it afterwards. The military calls it bottom line up front; journalism calls it the inverted pyramid; Minto calls it the governing thought. Three domains, one move, and the single highest-leverage edit available to a time-poor executive.
principles: Run the Reverse Outline on every memo and talk draft; it is the only diagnostic that reads your talk the way your audience reads it.
Front-load the recommendation in the first sixty seconds of any decision talk, then spend the remainder earning it.
State recommendations as commitments - 'we should fund X' - not as options for the room to consider.
If the work is genuinely exploratory, say so and still lead with the finding rather than the method.
Repair a buried conclusion in three edits: move the recommendation to sentence one, convert each section into a reason the recommendation follows, and signpost the count.

pitfalls.failure: Running a reverse outline on a talk you have already rehearsed to death, and finding that your three arguments are one argument plus two supporting facts.
pitfalls.fix: That is exactly what the diagnostic is for. Run it before rehearsal, then re-run it on the transcript after delivery - the transcript never lies about your order.

pitfalls.failure: Leading with the recommendation but with no bridge from it to the evidence, so the room treats it as an assertion and hunts for reasons to reject it.
pitfalls.fix: Keep the bridge in one sentence: 'We should fund X because Y, and here is how we know.' The answer comes first; the reasoning is not optional.

pitfalls.failure: Burying the conclusion in a meeting you assumed was exploratory, when the room had booked it to decide.
pitfalls.fix: Before presenting, ask one person what they expect to leave with. If they say a decision, the conclusion goes first regardless of how exploratory the work feels to you.

pitfalls.failure: Treating a soft conclusion as diplomacy, when a soft conclusion reads as indecision to a senior room.
pitfalls.fix: Commit to the recommendation. You can be uncertain about the reasoning - name that uncertainty explicitly - but never about what you are asking for.

concepts.title: StoryCircle and the Decision Arc: When Narrative Beats Argument
concepts.summary: Dan Harmon, the writer of Community and co-host of the Adventure Zone, published a compact account of story shape called the StoryCircle on Tumblr in 2011 and developed it further in his later writing, including Hunt a Thief (2020). Its eight beats describe a character with a want meeting resistance - which, mapped onto business, is a decision arc: the exact structure you need when the task is change rather than adjudication.
concepts.detail:
Harmon's eight steps: a character (you) is in a situation; the situation is characterised by a desire or goad; the character meets other characters; those characters hinder the desire (or goad it); the character therefore takes action toward a goal; that action meets resistance; the resistance motivates the character further; the cycle culminates in a dramatic resolution.

Mapped onto a business talk, the decision arc looks like this: the character is the audience, or you, or the customer; the situation is the world as it currently is; the desire is what they are trying to reach; the obstruction is the real resistance - status quo, a competing priority, a switching cost, internal politics, or a belief you have already failed to move; the action is what you are proposing; the resistance is why it is not happening today; the escalation is what happens if nothing changes, or what it costs to try; the resolution is the new equilibrium you are asking for.

The critical distinction is between a story about a customer and a decision arc. A customer story ('Sarah used our product and loved it') is illustration; it sits inside an argument as evidence. A decision arc ('Sarah has the same problem every quarter, tried three internal fixes, and the reason none of them worked is X') is a different structure, one that lets the audience locate themselves in a sequence of resistance rather than being lectured about a conclusion.

So when does narrative beat argument? When the task is to move people toward change - adoption, a new category, a cultural shift, a reorganisation, a strategy that requires people to give up something. When the audience already agrees with you but is not moving, an argument adds nothing, because there is no disagreement to resolve; there is inertia to dramatise. Nancy Duarte's Resonate (2010) frames the same tension as an oscillation between 'what is' and 'what could be'.

And when does argument beat narrative? Whenever the room is adjudicating: a recommendation, a budget, a plan, an audit, a comparison, a risk decision. A story there reads as persuasion without evidence, and a room trained to evaluate will start evaluating the story instead of the proposal.

The safe hybrid, and the one to default to: narrative in the first two minutes to establish situation and tension, then the deductive argument and the ask. The failure mode to avoid is narrativising the data - a chart cannot be a character, and a customer who is also a metric will convince nobody.
principles: Choose narrative when the task is change and inertia is the obstacle; choose argument when the task is adjudication and evidence is what is missing.
Map the decision arc explicitly: character, desire, obstruction, action, resistance, escalation, resolution - then check that each beat is on the page.
Use narrative for setup and argument for the ask; the two in sequence are stronger than either alone.
Never narrativise the data: charts and metrics stay in the argument, characters stay in the story.
Make the resolution a decision the audience can make, not a feeling the audience can admire.

pitfalls.failure: Opening a budget review with a customer story, so the room spends five minutes emotionally invested in a case they will not act on.
pitfalls.fix: Name the decision before the story and put a time on the story: two minutes maximum, then the argument.

pitfalls.failure: Using narrative to cover for missing evidence, so the story does the work the data should have done.
pitfalls.fix: Test the argument without the story: if the recommendation collapses, you have a data problem, and no amount of narrative will fix it.

pitfalls.failure: Building a hero narrative in which the customer is the hero, which quietly makes the audience the audience - the wrong dynamic for change.
pitfalls.fix: Put the audience in the hero seat: they are the person with the want, you are the guide who knows the path. That is the shape of most adoption.

pitfalls.failure: No resistance in the story, so the narrative feels like an advertisement and the room discounts it.
pitfalls.fix: Give the obstruction real weight, including the objection your audience would raise. Believable resistance is what makes a resolution credible.

concepts.title: From Brain Dump to Spine: The 20-Minute Raw Capture and the Shaping Pass
concepts.summary: The most reliable way to build a talk is to stop trying to build one and instead dump everything out, then shape. The raw capture is 20 minutes of unstructured writing or talking with no editing; the shaping pass is a separate, ruthless, 40-minute process that cuts, clusters, climbs the So-What Ladder, and produces the spine. Mixing the two modes destroys both.
concepts.detail:
There are two modes of work, and they have opposite rules. **Generative** mode is for producing material: no editing, no stopping, no structure, no judgement. **Editorial** mode is for shaping material: no new material, no exceptions. The most common failure in executive preparation is running both at once - pausing to restructure mid-dump, or adding new thoughts while editing. You get neither the raw material nor the structure, and you exhaust the time budget in the process.

**The 20-minute raw capture.** Set a timer for twenty minutes. Write or speak continuously, in whatever form comes out, with three prompts on the page and no more:

1. *What happened* - the facts, the numbers, the dates, the names, the quotes from people, the moments that surprised you. Specificity is only available in this pass; it is not available later from memory.
2. *What it means* - your read, your interpretation, the pattern you think you are seeing, the reasons.
3. *What you want* - what you want the room to think, feel, and do.

Do not organise. Do not stop to make a slide. Do not write a summary at the end. If you run out of things to say, describe the room, the weather, what you ate. Raw material is cheap; structure is what is scarce.

**The shaping pass.** A separate forty-minute block. Five moves, in order:

1. *Mark* - underline every claim in the dump. Facts are not claims.
2. *Cluster* - group the claims, looking for the MECE grouping that covers the question.
3. *Climb* - run the So-What Ladder on each cluster until it reaches a load-bearing claim.
4. *Select* - choose one governing thought. Cut everything that does not support it. Keep a parking lot for the cut material; you will need it in the Q and A.
5. *Sequence* - write the spine: governing thought, ask, three arguments, evidence, counter-argument, opening line, closing line.

Then, and only then, open the slide tool.

The two-pass structure also solves a subtler problem: writing prose first forces you to sentence every thought, and sentences commit you to a form of argument before you know what it is. Notes and fragments do not commit you. A dump in fragments can be reorganised; a dump in finished paragraphs usually cannot - which is why many executives find that their first draft sounds confident and wrong, and then spend the day rewriting sentences instead of fixing the structure underneath them.
principles: Separate generative work from editorial work in time and on paper; never run both in the same sitting.
Capture in fragments, not sentences - prose commits you to an argument before you have found it.
Use the three prompts (what happened, what it means, what you want) and resist adding a fourth.
Save specificity in the raw pass - numbers, names, dates - because it is not recoverable later from memory.
Keep a parking lot for cut material; it becomes your Q and A ammunition and your appendix.

pitfalls.failure: Writing the deck first and treating the raw dump as a script for slides, so the structure was fixed before the thinking was finished.
pitfalls.fix: Do the dump in a text document with the slide tool closed. The deck is the last artefact, not the first.

pitfalls.failure: Ending the dump with a tidy summary, which is where the energy stops and nothing is gained.
pitfalls.fix: Stop at the timer even mid-sentence. The raw pass should end abruptly; the shaping pass is where coherence gets imposed.

pitfalls.failure: Skipping the shaping pass because the dump already felt good in the moment.
pitfalls.fix: The dump always feels good - it is unexamined. Insist on the separate 40-minute editorial block, even if it means the talk is ready on a Friday and the spine is not.

pitfalls.failure: Cutting during the dump, so you lose the half-formed thought that contained the actual insight.
pitfalls.fix: Never cut in the dump. Only cut in the shaping pass, where you can see what the whole pile supports.
